# 03 — Reconstructing the method problem

**Question this document answers.** Why did an attempt to apply David's framework to four legal instruments with AI assistance become methodologically elaborate, when the framework itself is clearly specified?

**Position in the hierarchy.** Everything below is a problem *generated by applying* David's framework at scale with a language model. It is not an alternative framework. Where a control is described, the manuscript section it operationalizes is cited.

---

## 1. Why simple extraction was not enough

The framework's inference ladder (§6.2) is: legal text → institutional statements → governance relationships → governance configurations → legal architecture → governance regimes. Extraction — identifying the text, parsing statements, typing relations — is the part a language model does comparatively well and the part on which the two reconstructions agreed most.

The evidence for that is direct. Of 264 comparative units across the four cases, **one** material difference arose at the evidence level C0. At the relational level C1, 30 of 83 units differed materially. At C2, C3 and C4 together, 65 of 131 did. The disagreement is not about what the instruments say. It is about what may be built from what they say.

This is what the framework predicts. §6.6 calls the move from configurations to architecture "the most demanding inferential transition"; §6.2 says movement between levels "constitutes inference rather than mechanical transformation"; §6.8 names six recurrent ways the inference fails. The pilot's difficulty was not a failure to follow the framework. It was the discovery that the framework's *inference rules*, stated as principles, do not by themselves determine an output when a model has to produce one — and that a model asked for an architecture will produce an architecture.

---

## 2. The decisions that are not lexical extraction

Each of the following had to be decided, in every case, before any architectural statement could be written. None is recoverable from the text by reading alone. Each is a point where an AI-assisted coder will silently supply a default unless something stops it.

### 2.1 Configuration membership
Which relations belong to the same arrangement? The framework requires "a theoretically specified combination" (§6.5) and a membership rule, but the specification is per-domain. In the AI Act the two arms produced 3 configurations and 19 subconfigurations from the same relations; the contested membership questions were where designation of notified bodies, operator duties toward authorities and incident reporting belong (card HQ-AI-12). Nothing in the text assigns them.

### 2.2 Relation coupling
Is a link between two arrangements a coupling that makes them one, or an interface between two? The framework requires evidence that configurations are "sufficiently recurrent, consequential, necessary or structurally positioned" (§6.7, fourth rule) and warns that a shared actor is not enough. Operationalizing "enough" is the single largest source of divergence: 23 material differences at C3, and in the controlled arm 9 of 21 architecture candidates ended `INDETERMINATE` precisely on the coupling-consequence question.

### 2.3 Architecture boundaries
Where does one architecture end? Here the framework is unusually explicit: the **container fallacy** (§6.8) is "assuming that provisions located within the same legal act necessarily constitute a single coherent governance architecture." An AI-assisted run that is asked to reconstruct the architecture of an instrument has a structural bias toward exactly that fallacy, because the instrument is the prompt's unit. Three of the four cases produced a HIGH-priority card on this question alone (HQ-SCF-02, HQ-CBAM-10, HQ-AI-14).

### 2.4 External legal dependencies
What happens when the actors or devices that carry a configuration are constituted outside the instrument? Two concrete instances:
- CBAM: the status "accredited verifier" arises from accreditation under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/2067, and "national accreditation body" is constituted by Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 Art. 4(1). The Regulation governs through verifiers whose constitution is elsewhere.
- Directive 86/361/EEC: what counts as an "approved testing laboratory" is fixed by the CEPT accreditation system, and a NET's legal constitution rests on a Memorandum of Understanding between CEPT signatories. Both outside the Directive.

Across the four cases the controlled arm recorded 148 external references, **73 constitutive**, none verified (retrieval was not authorized). 19 of the 56 review cards turn on external evidence. A reconstruction that does not mark these will describe an architecture that the instrument does not, by itself, constitute.

### 2.5 Legal reference date and status
The four instruments were coded as **original acts as published**, not consolidated law. Directive 86/361/EEC was repealed in 1992. Nothing in a reconstruction reveals that unless the reference date is a declared field. An architectural claim without a date is a claim about no particular law.

### 2.6 Attribution of local properties to larger structures
Which property belongs to the whole rather than to each part? This is David's ecological fallacy (§6.8) and his requirement of a property bearer and scale (§6.6). In the AI Act the controlled arm found I3 `NOT_SATISFIED` for the instrument as a whole: no property attributable to the Regulation as such. The baseline attributed "differentiated, hybrid and multilevel" to the Regulation with high confidence. Same relations, opposite attribution decision.

### 2.7 Uncertainty
Assertiveness is not a property of the evidence; it is a property of the output. Pre-adjudication, calibration could not even be assessed in 93 of 96 material units (D6 `INDETERMINATE`). A model will produce fluent, confident prose about an architecture whether or not the warrant exists. Unless uncertainty is a recorded field with its own vocabulary, it disappears into adverbs.

### 2.8 Stopping rules
§6.10 asks: "what is the highest-level claim that the available evidence presently warrants?" As a principle this is clear. As an output it needs a place to be written. The pilot's clearest single instance: for Directive 86/361/EEC the controlled arm recorded `highest_level_reached = S` — it stopped below architecture. The baseline, reading the same twelve articles, asserted an architecture with high confidence while its own stopping record acknowledged that the Directive does not establish the significance or substitutability of the laboratories. Both are defensible readings of the same framework. The difference is that one procedure had a field in which "stop here" was an available answer.

### 2.9 Architecture candidate versus accepted architecture
A grouping that *might* be an architecture and a grouping that *is* one are different objects. The framework implies the distinction (§6.10's graded inference) but does not name it. Without the distinction, a candidate becomes an architecture by being written down. The Round-1 QA report flags this explicitly as a comparison hazard: raw candidate rows and higher-order inferences "are compared as inferences; none is treated as accepted before adjudication."

---

## 3. Where AI-assisted coding becomes vulnerable to unsupported inference

Three vulnerabilities, each specific to doing this work with a language model rather than a human coder.

**Fluency substitutes for warrant.** The output of an architectural inference is prose. A model generates well-formed architectural prose from thin evidence as readily as from thick evidence, and the prose carries no signal of which it was. A human coder who is unsure writes awkwardly or stops; a model does not.

**The prompt's unit becomes the answer's unit.** Ask for "the architecture of this Regulation" and you will receive one architecture per Regulation. This is the container fallacy arriving as an artefact of task framing. It is the single most consequential vulnerability found, and it accounts for three of the four architectural cards.

**Completion pressure runs upward.** The ladder's levels are hierarchically arranged, so a model treats the top as the goal. `INDETERMINATE` and "stop at the configuration level" are not natural completions of a task whose stated object is an architecture. They have to be made available as outputs, or they will not occur.

A fourth vulnerability is a property of this pilot rather than of AI coding generally, and must be stated: both arms and the comparator ran on the same model. The exercise therefore cannot distinguish the effect of the controls from the effect of a longer, more structured prompt. Nothing in the pilot measures that difference.

---

## 4. What the controls are, and what they are not

The crosswalk frozen before the comparison (`V8_RGAM_METHOD_CROSSWALK.md`) compared the two procedures element by element. Its verdicts are the clearest available statement of the intellectual relationship:

- `EQUIVALENT` in conceptual function for: source and coverage declaration; institutional statements; normative assignment without a counterparty; qualified relations; candidate configurations; positional properties; whole-level properties; **architectural inference (I1–I4 against David's §6.2/§6.6)**; boundary, alternative and sensitivity control; evidential status; the stopping rule; human review; multidimensional profiles without a score.
- `PARTIAL_OVERLAP` for: actor/position; function; mechanism; instrument; the authority/discretion/accountability attributes; architecture-versus-regime.
- `NO_DEFENSIBLE_EQUIVALENT` for: David's **object** category, which the controlled arm has no homologous stratum for — a gap on the controlled side, not an addition.
- `METHOD_SPECIFIC` for: David's strategies and governance logics, which the controlled arm excluded from basic coding.

So the additional machinery is, on its own prospective account, mostly the same requirements written as mandatory fields with a controlled vocabulary and an authorized set of outcomes. The additions are: **a field where "stop" and "indeterminate" are legal answers**, **a candidate status that must be earned**, and **a rival-grouping and defeater record that must be filled**. The subtractions are: David's object layer, and his strategy and logic layer.

That is the honest description. The controls did not extend the framework. They made some of its requirements unavoidable for a machine executor, at a procedural cost documented in `05_METHOD_CONTROLS_REVIEW.md`.

---

## 5. The proposition this pilot was used to test

> The difficult part is not the extraction of relations but the control of inferential transitions between analytical levels.

**Supported, with one important qualification.**

Supported by: the distribution of material differences (1 at C0; 65 of 96 at C2–C4); the concentration of HIGH-priority cards on architecture existence, number and boundary (H5 on 12 cards, H6 on 11, H11 on 14); and four of the six reported decisions turning on exactly the configuration→architecture transition.

Qualified by: the transitions are not uniformly difficult, and control is not uniformly beneficial. In the six validated cards the controls were endorsed where they **restrained an upward inference** (C3) or **enforced a named party** (C1), and not endorsed where they **subdivided a representation that was already adequate** (C2, HQ-AI-12). The more precise proposition the pilot supports is therefore:

> The vulnerable operation is the *upward* transition from configuration to architecture and from architecture to governance proposition, where a machine executor will complete what the evidence does not warrant. Finer *downward* decomposition at the configuration level is a different operation, and the pilot gives one direct instance in which it did not help.
